Welcome back. Everything on this page runs real R in your browser — same setup as the other coding activities. **Errors are normal.** When R stops with red text, it is telling you something specific went wrong. Your job is to read that message, fix the line, and check that the fix worked.

The first time you click **Run Code**, your browser downloads R once (a few seconds). After that it is quick.

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read an error message

R prints errors from the **inside out**:

1. **Start at the bottom line** — that is usually what went wrong (`object 'x' not found`, `could not find function`, and so on).
2. **Read upward** for the **line number** and **function name** where R got stuck.
3. **Fix one thing**, run again, and see whether the message changes.

Errors are information, not failure. Every experienced programmer sees them all day.
:::

## 1. Object not found

### See the error

Someone tried to compute the mean body mass of penguins. Run their code below.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
mean(body_mass)
```

Read the bottom line of the error: **`object 'body_mass' not found`**. R is telling you that name was never created in memory — but **what should `body_mass` have been?**

### Inspect the data

Before you fix anything, load the penguins dataset and see which columns are available. Run **`library(palmerpenguins)`** and **`glimpse(penguins)`** below. Look for a body-mass column measured in grams.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
glimpse(penguins)
```

### Fix the code

Now write code that creates `body_mass` from the right column and computes its mean in grams.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: fix_object_not_found
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_object_not_found
mean(body_mass)
```

::: {.hint exercise="fix_object_not_found"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

R looks up object names in memory. If you see `object '...' not found`, create the object with `<-` before you use it.

From your `glimpse(penguins)` output, find the body-mass column measured in grams — its name ends in `_g`.

Example with `mtcars`:

```r
mpg_vals <- mtcars$mpg
mean(mpg_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Apply the same two-step pattern: assign that column from `penguins`, then call `mean()` on it.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="fix_object_not_found"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

R looks up names in memory. If `body_mass` was never assigned, R cannot find it.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_object_not_found
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("body_mass\\s*<-", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Create `body_mass` first with `<-` before you call `mean()` on it."
  )
} else if (!grepl("body_mass_g", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Pull the column from `penguins` with `penguins$body_mass_g`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0("Fixed. Mean body mass: ", round(.last_value, 1), " g.")
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "You got `NA` because two penguins have missing weights. Add `na.rm = TRUE` inside `mean()`."
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Assign `body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g`, then call `mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
}
```

## 2. Wrong column name

This line fails because the column name is slightly wrong. Fix it and run `head()` on the result to confirm you have numbers.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_column_name
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass
head(body_mass)
```

::: {.hint exercise="fix_column_name"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The `$` operator pulls one column from a data frame. Column names must match **exactly** — run `?Extract` or inspect names first:

```r
glimpse(mtcars)
head(mtcars$mpg)
```

If `$` returns `NULL`, the name is wrong. Use `glimpse()` on `penguins` to find the correct body-mass column name.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="fix_column_name"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
head(body_mass)
```

`$` returns `NULL` when the column name does not match exactly — R is case-sensitive and picky about spelling.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_column_name
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("body_mass_g", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "The correct column name is `body_mass_g`, not `body_mass`."
  )
} else if (exists("body_mass", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  bm <- get("body_mass", envir = .envir_result)
  if (is.numeric(bm) && length(bm) == 344) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "Column name fixed — 344 numeric values, as expected."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Use `penguins$body_mass_g` to get the full numeric column."
    )
  }
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Assign `body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g` and run `head(body_mass)`."
  )
}
```

## 3. Function typo

`filtr` is not a real function. Fix the typo, keep only Adelie penguins, and run the line.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: fix_function_typo
library(dplyr)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_function_typo
adelie <- filtr(penguins, species == "Adelie")
adelie
```

::: {.hint exercise="fix_function_typo"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

`could not find function "..."` usually means a typo in the function name. From `?filter`: `filter(.data, ..., .preserve = FALSE)`.

Correct spelling example:

```r
filter(mtcars, cyl == 4)
```

Compare your function name letter by letter with the dplyr verb for keeping rows.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="fix_function_typo"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
adelie <- filter(penguins, species == "Adelie")
adelie
```

`could not find function "filtr"` means R has no function with that exact name — often a one-letter typo.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_function_typo
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (grepl("filtr\\s*\\(", code) && !grepl("filter\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Change `filtr` to `filter`."
  )
} else if (!grepl("filter\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `filter()` to keep rows where `species == \"Adelie\"`."
  )
} else if (exists("adelie", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  ad <- get("adelie", envir = .envir_result)
  if (is.data.frame(ad) && nrow(ad) > 100 && all(ad$species == "Adelie")) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = paste0("Fixed. ", nrow(ad), " Adelie penguins — filter worked.")
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Filter to Adelie with `filter(penguins, species == \"Adelie\")`."
    )
  }
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Save the result as `adelie` and display it."
  )
}
```

## 4. Type mismatch

Run this broken line on purpose. Read the error, then fix it so R averages a **numeric column**, not text in quotes.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_type_mismatch
mean("3500")
```

::: {.hint exercise="fix_type_mismatch"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?mean`: the first argument must be **numeric**. Text in quotes is character, not a number.

Broken vs. fixed pattern:

```r
mean("20")                      # character — wrong type
mean(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)  # numeric column — correct type
```

Pass a numeric column from `penguins`, not a quoted string.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="fix_type_mismatch"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
```

`non-numeric argument to binary operator` (or similar) means R expected a number and got something else — often quotes around a value that should be numeric.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_type_mismatch
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (grepl('mean\\s*\\(\\s*"', code) || grepl("mean\\s*\\(\\s*'", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Remove the quotes — pass a numeric column, not a text string."
  )
} else if (grepl("body_mass_g", code) && grepl("mean\\s*\\(", code)) {
  if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "Numeric mean computed — type mismatch resolved."
    )
  } else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && is.na(.last_value)) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Add `na.rm = TRUE` so missing weights are skipped."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Run `mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)`."
    )
  }
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Use `mean()` on `penguins$body_mass_g`, not on quoted text."
  )
}
```

## 5. Missing `na.rm = TRUE`

This runs without crashing but returns `NA`. Fix it so R skips missing values and returns the actual average.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_na_rm
mean(penguins$body_mass_g)
```

::: {.hint exercise="fix_na_rm"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?mean`: `mean(x, na.rm = FALSE)` — when `na.rm = FALSE` (the default), any missing value makes the whole result `NA`.

Example:

```r
mean(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Add `na.rm = TRUE` to your `mean()` call on the penguin body-mass column.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="fix_na_rm"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Two penguins have missing body mass. Without `na.rm = TRUE`, `mean()` returns `NA` rather than guessing.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: fix_na_rm
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("na\\.rm\\s*=\\s*TRUE", code, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Add `na.rm = TRUE` inside `mean()`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0("Average: ", round(.last_value, 1), " g — missing values skipped.")
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Use `mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
}
```

## 6. Test that your fix worked

Fixing a line is not the end. **Verify** before you move on:

- Re-run the line that failed
- Use `glimpse()` or `str()` to confirm structure
- After a `filter()`, check `nrow()` — did you keep the rows you expected?
- Use `print()` or `head()` when output looks suspicious

Below is a working filter that drops penguins with missing body mass. Add a line that prints **how many rows** remain. You should see **342**.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: verify_nrow
library(dplyr)
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g))
```

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: verify_nrow
# Check how many rows remain:

```

::: {.hint exercise="verify_nrow"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?nrow`: `nrow(x)` returns the number of rows in a data frame — a quick check after `filter()`.

Example:

```r
mtcars |>
  filter(cyl == 4) |>
  nrow()
```

Count rows in the filtered penguin object named in the exercise.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="verify_nrow"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
nrow(penguins_clean)
```

342 rows — two penguins with missing body mass were removed. Row counts are a fast sanity check after every filter or join.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
#| exercise: verify_nrow
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("nrow\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `nrow(penguins_clean)` to count rows."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && .last_value == 342) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = "342 rows — filter worked as expected. Good verification habit."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = paste0("Got ", .last_value, " rows — expected 342 after dropping missing body mass.")
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Run `nrow(penguins_clean)` and confirm the count."
  )
}
```

## 7. Where to get help (without AI)

When you are stuck after reading the error and trying a fix:

- **Read the error again** — bottom line first, then line number
- **Help pages:** `?mean`, `?filter` (dense, but official)
- **Web search:** paste the **exact error text** in quotes
- **Compare** your line to a working example from lecture, an activity, or a classmate
- **Ask a human:** office hours, discussion board, instructor, or TA

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Try this with a partner.** One person reads the error message aloud slowly; the other suggests what to try first. Swap roles. Saying the error out loud often makes the fix obvious.
:::

## 8. Using generative AI to debug

Generative AI can explain errors in plain language — if you give it enough context. Copy a prompt like this into ChatGPT, Claude, or another tool (when your syllabus allows it):

> I am a beginner learning R in an introductory biology course. Here is the code I ran, the full error message, and what I was trying to do: \[paste code\], \[paste error\], \[one sentence goal\]. Please explain the error in plain language, suggest one fix, and show a corrected example using the Palmer Penguins dataset. Do not write my graded assignment for me.

**Rules that keep AI useful and honest:**

- Paste **your** code and the **full** error — not just "it doesn't work"
- **Run** the suggested fix yourself before submitting anything graded
- **Disclose** AI use on assignments when the syllabus requires it

## 9. Course tools you can use

BILD 5 offers several AI-related resources. Names only — your instructor or Canvas will show you where to find each one:

| Tool | What it is for |
|------|----------------|
| **BILD5 bug checker chatbot** | Course-specific help with R error messages and debugging steps |
| **Schema Study** | Socratic study coach for biology concepts — good for understanding *what* you are analyzing, not for pasting quiz or exam questions |
| **Triton GPT** | UC San Diego's campus AI assistant — general help; still verify any code yourself and follow the course AI policy |

None of these replace running and testing your own code. They supplement the read → fix → verify workflow you practiced above.

## 10. Recap

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The debug workflow

1. **Read** the error (bottom line, then line number)
2. **Fix** one thing at a time
3. **Test** — re-run, check `nrow()`, `glimpse()`, or `head()`
4. **Ask for help** — human, help page, search, or AI with full context

If you can do this on your own with Palmer penguins, you can do it on Coding Assignments and in DataHub.
:::

## Keep playing

Intentionally break a line, read the error, and fix it without looking at the hints. For example, typo a column name or forget `na.rm = TRUE`.

```{webr}
#| envir: debug_lab
# Break this on purpose, then fix it:
mean(penguins$flipper_lenght_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
The column is `flipper_length_mm` — not `flipper_lenght_mm`. Practice the full loop: run, read, fix, verify.
:::
